title: 80% of People Aren't Getting Enough of the Nutrient That Protects Hearts and Brains — Even If They Eat Their Five a Day
excerpt: A 30,000-person urine analysis published in Food & Function found that fewer than one in five people consume the 500mg daily flavanol target linked to slower cognitive decline and lower cardiovascular risk — and the fix may be as simple as a cup of green tea.
body:
A massive new study has exposed a nutrient gap hiding in plain sight — one that even health-conscious eaters are falling into.

Researchers from Harvard Medical School and the University of Reading analysed urine samples from 30,000 people across the UK and United States, bypassing the unreliable self-reporting that plagues most dietary studies. Their findings, published in *Food & Function*, revealed that a staggering 80 per cent of participants were not consuming enough flavanols — a group of plant compounds increasingly linked to better heart health and slower brain ageing.

The recommended daily intake is 500mg, and while that is "perfectly possible to get from a normal diet," study co-author Professor Gunter Kuhnle noted, "fewer than one in five participants actually did this — even among those who ate their five a day."

What Are Flavanols — and Why Should You Care?

Flavanols are a subset of flavonoids, the compounds that give fruits and vegetables their vivid colours. They are found in especially high concentrations in green tea, dark chocolate, berries, apples, and plums. Paler produce — cauliflower, potatoes, iceberg lettuce — contains far less.

The health payoff from adequate flavanol intake is substantial. A landmark Harvard study (the COSMOS trial, involving 21,000 participants over three years) found that flavanol supplementation reduced cardiovascular disease risk. A related cognitive sub-study showed that people with low baseline flavanol intake who were given supplements experienced measurable improvements in memory.

A 2020 study in *Scientific Reports* demonstrated that flavanol-rich cocoa beverages increased cerebral blood flow and improved cognitive performance in healthy adults — effectively "equalising" lower-performing participants with their sharper peers.

The Five-a-Day Trap

The study's most provocative finding is that meeting standard dietary guidelines — the familiar "five portions of fruit and vegetables a day" — does not guarantee adequate flavanol intake. "A random selection of five fruits and veg each day is unlikely to provide meaningful amounts," Kuhnle warned.

This is because flavanol content varies enormously between foods. A cup of green tea can contain over 300mg of flavanols. A serving of blackberries delivers roughly 100mg. But a banana or a carrot contributes almost nothing.

Lead author Javier Ottaviani put the fix in practical terms: "A handful of blackberries, a whole apple, or having a cup of green tea alongside your meal makes a real difference."

The South Asian Advantage — If You Use It

For the Indian diaspora, this research carries a particular resonance. Traditional Indian diets are already rich in several flavanol sources that Western diets typically lack. Green tea, pomegranates, amla (Indian gooseberry), and dark spices like cinnamon all contribute meaningful flavanol doses. The habit of ending a meal with green tea or chai made with real tea leaves — not just milk and sugar — is a built-in advantage.

But the shift toward processed and convenience foods among second-generation NRIs in the US and UK may be eroding that advantage. Studies tracking dietary patterns in South Asian diaspora communities consistently show declining fruit and vegetable diversity and increased reliance on packaged snacks — a combination that makes flavanol deficiency more likely, not less.

The metabolic context makes this especially concerning. South Asians already face elevated cardiovascular and diabetes risk at lower BMI thresholds than other populations. A nutrient that demonstrably improves vascular function and cerebral blood flow is not a luxury — it is a dietary priority.

What to Eat

The highest-impact flavanol sources, according to the study, include:

  • **Green tea** (~300mg per cup)
  • **Dark chocolate** (at least 70% cocoa, ~100mg per 20g)
  • **Blackberries** (~100mg per serving)
  • **Apples with skin** (~50mg each)
  • **Cranberries and plums** (~50-80mg per serving)
  • **Cherries** (~40mg per serving)

The study authors stopped short of recommending flavanol supplements, noting that whole-food sources carry additional fibre, vitamins, and other bioactives that supplements cannot replicate.

The Bottom Line

Eating your vegetables is necessary but not sufficient. *Which* vegetables — and which fruits, and whether you drink tea — matters at least as much as how many servings you check off. The 80 per cent of us who are flavanol-deficient are not unhealthy eaters; we are just eating the wrong plants.

Sources: *Food & Function* (2026), Ottaviani et al.; COSMOS Trial, Harvard/Brigham and Women's Hospital; *Scientific Reports* (2020), University of Birmingham
